add_eyes.name: Valentine Gross (later Valentine Hugo)
add_eyes.role: Painter and illustrator, aged 25; a regular at the Ballets Russes who drew the dancers during performances and rehearsals
add_eyes.side: Paris artists around the Ballets Russes
add_eyes.where: In the house at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, drawing
add_eyes.vantage_label: the eye with a pencil in the dark
add_eyes.authenticity: Her sketches and pastels of the Rite are in the Valentine Gross Archive at the V&A (THM/165, given by Jean Hugo), with others in Paris collections. The V&A says she made preliminary sketches during performances and rehearsals between 1909 and 1919 and worked some up later into finished pencil or colour drawings, so not every sheet is a same-night record. A drawing of Maria Piltz in the Sacrificial Dance is dated 29 May 1913 and was published in Montjoie! in June 1913.
add_eyes.bio: Nijinsky's choreography was never filmed and left the repertoire within a year. Gross's quick drawings of the Chosen One, the Old Woman and the circling maidens are among the few images of it made while it was being danced. In 1987 the reconstruction by Millicent Hodson and Kenneth Archer relied heavily on them.

sources.title: V&A: Le Sacre du Printemps, pastel by Valentine Gross (S.643-1989)
Numeridanse webdoc: Rite of passage (Gross drawing of Piltz, 29 May 1913)

add_eyes.name: Giacomo Puccini
add_eyes.role: Italian opera composer, aged 54, in Paris in early June 1913
add_eyes.where: In the audience at a later performance, Théâtre des Champs-Élysées
add_eyes.vantage_label: the rival master in the stalls
add_eyes.authenticity: Wikipedia's Rite of Spring article says Puccini attended the 2 June performance. His verdict is widely quoted in English from a letter usually said to be to Tito Ricordi, but the recipient, the exact date and the Italian original were not checked here. Treat it as reported, and quote only the much-repeated fragment.
add_eyes.bio: The most successful opera composer alive heard the Rite in its first week and called it, in effect, the work of a madman, while still granting it originality and talent. His reaction is the old theatre judging the new from inside the trade.

sources.title: The Rite of Spring (Wikipedia: Puccini at the 2 June performance)
uDiscover Music: The riot at the Rite of Spring premiere (Puccini's remark)

add_eyes.name: Pierre Lalo
add_eyes.role: Music critic of Le Temps, aged 47; son of the composer Édouard Lalo
add_eyes.where: Paris; reviewing the Rite and Jeux together
add_eyes.authenticity: His feuilleton 'La Musique' in Le Temps, 3 June 1913, is reproduced by the Presse musicale française project (OICRM). Digested, not quoted.
add_eyes.bio: Lalo was the most feared critic in Paris and a long-standing opponent of the Ballets Russes' cult of novelty. His review, written after the first week, separates music he respected from choreography he despised. That split ran through much of the reception.

sources.title: Pierre Lalo, 'La Musique', Le Temps, 3 June 1913 (Presse musicale française, OICRM)

add_eyes.name: Florent Schmitt
add_eyes.role: Composer and critic of La France, aged 42; friend of Stravinsky
add_eyes.where: In the house at the premiere; then at his critic's desk
add_eyes.form: newspaper review; anecdotes recorded by others later
add_eyes.authenticity: His review appeared in La France on 4 June 1913, as summarised by the Florent Schmitt website. The stories of him shouting at the boxes come from Stravinsky's 1962 commentary and Casella's 1955 memoir, both written decades later.
add_eyes.bio: Schmitt was one of the young Paris composers who championed Stravinsky. He heard the premiere as a call to arms, and his review was the most extravagant praise the work got that week. He is the defender's voice that Lalo and Quittard were answering.

sources.title: Florent Schmitt and Igor Stravinsky: a consequential musical relationship (florentschmitt.com)

add_entries.headline: Drawing the Chosen One while the house roars
add_entries.digest: While others argued in the aisles, Gross drew Maria Piltz, the Chosen One, in the Sacrificial Dance. The drawing is dated to the premiere night. Hers is the only record in this chapter made on the spot that shows the dance itself and not the audience.
add_entries.source_note: Numeridanse webdoc 'Rite of passage': Gross drawing of Marie Piltz in the Sacrificial Dance, drawn in Paris on 29 May 1913 and published in Montjoie! in June 1913.

add_entries.headline: Shouting down the boxes, by later accounts
add_entries.digest: By the later accounts of Casella (1955) and Stravinsky (1962), Schmitt stood up in the din and yelled insults at the society women of the expensive sixteenth arrondissement and at an old gentleman in a box. These are recollections decades after the fact, not his own record. They agree only that the young composers in the house fought back.
add_entries.source_note: florentschmitt.com (citing Stravinsky's 1962 commentary and Alfredo Casella's 1955 memoir). Later anecdote, flagged as such.

add_entries.place: Théâtre des Champs-Élysées; letter from Paris
add_entries.headline: Puccini hears a madman's cacophony, with talent in it
add_entries.digest: Puccini went to a later performance, given by Wikipedia as 2 June, and in a letter, usually said to be to Tito Ricordi, called the choreography ridiculous and the music sheer cacophony, the creation of a madman. He granted it some originality and real talent and reported a public that hissed, laughed and applauded. As always with this letter, recipient and date are as reported in secondary sources.
add_entries.source_note: Wikipedia, The Rite of Spring (Puccini at the 2 June performance); uDiscover Music (the 'work of a madman … sheer cacophony' remark). Letter recipient and date not checked against an Italian edition.

add_entries.headline: Le Temps: clever, dissonant music, ugly dancing
add_entries.digest: Lalo reviewed the Rite together with Debussy's Jeux. He judged the choreography a regrettable mediocrity in which everything was ugly, with neither grace nor expression. The music was skilful and ingenious but heavily dissonant, its daring more superficial than deep. He found the young musicians' talk of a masterpiece excessive, scolded the audience for its racket and discourtesy, and promised a closer look after another hearing.
add_entries.source_note: Pierre Lalo, 'La Musique', Le Temps, 3 June 1913 (Presse musicale française, OICRM, ART-LAP-1913-02). Paraphrased.

add_entries.headline: La France: the Messiah awaited since Wagner
add_entries.digest: A day after Lalo, Schmitt's review hailed the Rite as a summit of Russian art and the arrival of a new music. He set Stravinsky up as the composer the age had been waiting for since Wagner. Read beside Lalo and Quittard, it shows the premiere splitting Paris critics into two camps within a week.
add_entries.source_note: Florent Schmitt, review in La France, 4 June 1913, as summarised on florentschmitt.com. Paraphrased; no translation quoted.

add_entries.headline: Her drawings go to press in Montjoie!
add_entries.digest: Canudo's magazine Montjoie!, which had printed Stravinsky's statement on the day of the premiere, published Gross's drawing of the Sacrificial Dance in June. Readers who missed the four Paris performances could see the dance the critics were arguing over.
add_entries.source_note: Numeridanse webdoc 'Rite of passage' (publication in Montjoie!, June 1913); NYPL digital collections hold the Montjoie! run. Issue number not checked.

add_entries.date_display: 1913 (sketches made in the theatre, worked up later)
add_entries.headline: Pastels of the circling maidens, finished from the sketches
add_entries.digest: From her quick theatre studies Gross worked up a small pastel of the Glorification of the Chosen One: maidens in cream dresses with red trim and long black plaits in a ring, one figure standing alone at the centre against a blurred green ground. Other sheets catch the Old Woman bending, falling, scurrying and twisting. They record shapes and groupings that no film preserved.
add_entries.source_note: V&A S.643-1989 (pastel, 19 × 25 cm, Valentine Gross Archive THM/165); the V&A says she sketched in performances and rehearsals and worked the drawings up later. Exact date of the finished pastel unknown.

add_convergences.label: The first week's verdicts: stalls, studio and press
add_convergences.note: Between 2 and 4 June Van Vechten is being drummed on in the stalls, Puccini is calling it a madman's cacophony, Lalo in Le Temps dismisses the dancing as ugly, and Schmitt in La France hails a Messiah. Gross, meanwhile, is turning her theatre sketches into the images that would outlast the choreography. They saw the same performances and drew opposite lessons.

add_ties.note: Gross drew Nijinsky's dancers in performance. Her drawings became a main source for the 1987 reconstruction of his lost choreography.
Friends and allies in Paris. Schmitt defended the Rite in the house and in print, and Stravinsky later recalled his shouting.
In consecutive days' papers (3 and 4 June 1913), Le Temps called the dancing ugly and the daring superficial, and La France proclaimed a new music.
Lalo's 3 June feuilleton reviewed Debussy's Jeux beside the Rite, judging the two Nijinsky ballets together.

add_threads_out.note: Debussy, who sight-read the Rite with Stravinsky in 1912 and saw Jeux and the Rite premiered two weeks apart, had heard the Javanese gamelan at the 1889 Exposition. His essay praising Javanese music came out early in 1913, the year of both ballets.

updates.why: Gross's drawing of the Sacrificial Dance is dated 29 May 1913 (Numeridanse). Schmitt's presence at the premiere is attested, though his shouting rests on later recollection (florentschmitt.com).
